title: DNA: The Code of Life

standard_text: The structure of DNA and RNA; the location of DNA (nucleus, mitochondria, chloroplasts); DNA replication; protein synthesis: transcription and translation; the genetic code; DNA profiling and its uses. (summary of CAPS Life Sciences, Grade 12, Life Sciences: DNA: the code of life)
meta_desc: Free Grade 12 Life Sciences worksheets (CAPS): DNA and RNA, base pairing, replication, transcription, translation and DNA profiling. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: A pairs with T (in RNA, U); C pairs with G.
body_html:
How to think about it

DNA is a double helix of two strands of nucleotides (a sugar, a phosphate and a base). The bases pair: adenine with thymine and cytosine with guanine, joined by hydrogen bonds. In replication the helix unwinds, and each strand is a template for a new strand (semi-conservative replication).

In transcription, a gene's DNA is copied into mRNA in the nucleus (U replaces T). In translation, ribosomes read the mRNA in codons of three bases; tRNA brings the matching amino acids, which are joined into a protein. DNA profiling compares DNA fragments to identify people, for paternity tests and in forensics.

Example

DNA strand ATG CCA. Complementary DNA?

A–T, C–G

Answer: TAC GGT

Example

DNA template TAC. mRNA codon?

U instead of T

Answer: AUG

Common mistakes

  • Pairing A with U in DNA.
  • Thinking proteins are made in the nucleus.
  • Mixing up codons (mRNA) and anticodons (tRNA).

faq.q: Why is DNA replication called semi-conservative?
faq.a: Each new DNA molecule has one old strand and one new strand.

faq.q: Is DNA profiling proof of guilt?
faq.a: It is strong evidence, but samples can be contaminated, so it is used with other evidence.

items.q: In the DNA of a fish, 27% of the bases are adenine. What percentage are adenine and thymine together?
A DNA molecule has 7 000 base pairs. How long is it? (distance between base pairs = 0,34 nm)
A DNA strand reads CAG TAC. What is the complementary DNA strand?
items.e: In DNA, A pairs with T and G pairs with C.

items.q: A DNA segment has 3 970 base pairs. How many hydrogen bonds hold it together if 30% of its bases are adenine?
items.e: A = T = 30%, G = C = 20%. A–T pairs = 2 382 (2 bonds), G–C pairs = 1588 (3 bonds): total = 9 528.

items.q: In a sample of double-stranded DNA, 32% of the bases are adenine (A). What percentage are thymine (T)?
items.e: A pairs with T, so T = 32%. A + T = 64%, so G + C = 36% and G = C = 18%.

items.q: In a sample of double-stranded DNA, 22% of the bases are adenine (A). What percentage are guanine (G)?
items.e: A pairs with T, so T = 22%. A + T = 44%, so G + C = 56% and G = C = 28%.

items.q: A DNA strand reads CTC AGG AGT. What is the complementary DNA strand?
items.e: In DNA, A pairs with T and G pairs with C.

items.e: A pairs with T, so T = 22%. A + T = 44%, so G + C = 56% and G = C = 28%.

In a sample of double-stranded DNA, 35% of the bases are adenine (A). What percentage are cytosine (C)?
items.e: A pairs with T, so T = 35%. A + T = 70%, so G + C = 30% and G = C = 15%.

items.q: In a sample of double-stranded DNA, 15% of the bases are adenine (A). What percentage are cytosine (C)?
items.e: A pairs with T, so T = 15%. A + T = 30%, so G + C = 70% and G = C = 35%.

items.e: A = T = 30%, G = C = 20%. A–T pairs = 1 326 (2 bonds), G–C pairs = 884 (3 bonds): total = 5 304.

items.q: In a sample of double-stranded DNA, 30% of the bases are adenine (A). What percentage are thymine (T)?
items.e: A pairs with T, so T = 30%. A + T = 60%, so G + C = 40% and G = C = 20%.

items.q: In a sample of double-stranded DNA, 28% of the bases are adenine (A). What percentage are guanine (G)?
items.e: A pairs with T, so T = 28%. A + T = 56%, so G + C = 44% and G = C = 22%.

items.q: A DNA strand reads TTC CTA. What is the complementary DNA strand?
items.e: In DNA, A pairs with T and G pairs with C.

items.q: In the DNA of a plant, 38% of the bases are adenine. What percentage are adenine and thymine together?
In the DNA of a plant, 33% of the bases are adenine. What percentage are guanine?
items.e: A + T = 66%, so G + C = 34%, and guanine = half of that: 17,0%.

items.q: What is translation?
c: making a polypeptide from the code in mRNA
items.e: It happens on ribosomes.

items.q: Why is the genetic code called degenerate?
c: most amino acids are coded by more than one codon
items.e: There are 61 sense codons for 20 amino acids.

items.q: One DNA strand has the base sequence CATCATCCCTTA. What is the sequence of the complementary strand?
items.e: A pairs with T and G pairs with C.

items.q: A section of double-stranded DNA is 300 base pairs long. How many nucleotides does it contain?
items.e: Each base pair is two nucleotides: 600.

items.q: A section of double-stranded DNA is 1 000 base pairs long. How many nucleotides does it contain?
items.e: Each base pair is two nucleotides: 2000.

items.q: Who is known for transformation in Streptococcus pneumoniae using mice?
items.e: Frederick Griffith: transformation in Streptococcus pneumoniae using mice.

items.q: A section of double-stranded DNA is 500 base pairs long. How many nucleotides does it contain?
items.e: Each base pair is two nucleotides: 1 000.

items.q: One DNA strand has the base sequence TGTTTCTAATCA. What is the sequence of the complementary strand?
items.e: A pairs with T and G pairs with C.

items.q: A section of double-stranded DNA is 200 base pairs long. How many nucleotides does it contain?
items.e: Each base pair is two nucleotides: 400.

items.q: One DNA strand has the base sequence TATTAGACC. What is the sequence of the complementary strand?
items.e: A pairs with T and G pairs with C.

items.q: One DNA strand has the base sequence AACGCCTG. What is the sequence of the complementary strand?
items.e: A pairs with T and G pairs with C.

items.q: What is Jacob and Monod known for?
c: the lac operon model of gene regulation
showing with bacteriophages that DNA is the genetic material
suggesting that the genetic code is made of three bases
items.e: Jacob and Monod: the lac operon model of gene regulation.

items.q: One DNA strand has the base sequence GGTCCACCTGCT. What is the sequence of the complementary strand?
items.e: A pairs with T and G pairs with C.

items.q: What is the function of tRNA?
c: it carries the code from DNA
it brings the correct amino acid to the ribosome by matching its anticodon to the codon
items.e: It has a clover-leaf shape.

items.q: What is Frederick Griffith known for?
c: showing with bacteriophages that DNA is the genetic material
the lac operon model of gene regulation
transformation in Streptococcus pneumoniae using mice
items.e: Frederick Griffith: transformation in Streptococcus pneumoniae using mice.

items.q: Who is known for the double-helix model of DNA?
items.e: Watson and Crick: the double-helix model of DNA.

items.q: A DNA segment has 1540 base pairs. How many hydrogen bonds hold it together if 30% of its bases are adenine?
items.e: A = T = 30%, G = C = 20%. A–T pairs = 924 (2 bonds), G–C pairs = 616 (3 bonds): total = 3 696.

items.q: What is splicing?
c: removing introns and joining exons in the primary RNA transcript of eukaryotes
items.e: A cap and a poly-A tail are also added.

items.q: What is the sugar in DNA?
items.e: RNA has ribose.

items.q: What is a VNTR?
c: a variable number of tandem repeats used in DNA fingerprinting
items.e: Their number differs between people.

items.q: One DNA strand has the base sequence GGTTTGCTCA. What is the sequence of the complementary strand?
items.e: A pairs with T and G pairs with C.

items.q: What is the genetic code?
c: the order of chromosomes in a cell
the sequence of base triplets (codons) that specifies amino acids
the number of genes in an organism
items.e: It is universal and degenerate.

items.q: What does semi-conservative replication mean?
c: both strands of the new molecule are new
each new DNA molecule has one original strand and one new strand
items.e: Shown by the Meselson–Stahl experiment.

items.q: A mRNA has a reading frame of 189 codons, the last being a stop codon. How many amino acids are in the polypeptide?
items.e: The stop codon codes for no amino acid: 188.

items.q: Which bases pair in DNA?
c: adenine with uracil, and cytosine with guanine
every base can pair with any other
adenine with thymine, and cytosine with guanine
adenine with cytosine, and guanine with thymine
items.e: A–T has two hydrogen bonds, C–G three.

items.q: How can two cells with the same DNA, such as a nerve cell and a muscle cell, be so different?
c: different genes are switched on (expressed) in each cell
one cell has lost its DNA
items.e: Gene regulation controls differentiation.

items.q: What is the start codon in mRNA?
items.e: UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons.

items.q: Why is the genetic code called degenerate?
c: each codon codes for several amino acids
most amino acids are coded for by more than one codon
items.e: There are 64 codons for 20 amino acids.

items.q: A polypeptide has 105 amino acids. How many nucleotides (excluding the stop codon) are needed in its mRNA?
items.e: Each amino acid needs one codon of three bases: 3 × 105 = 315.

items.q: A mRNA has a reading frame of 258 codons, the last being a stop codon. How many amino acids are in the polypeptide?
items.e: The stop codon codes for no amino acid: 257.

items.q: A mRNA has a reading frame of 81 codons, the last being a stop codon. How many amino acids are in the polypeptide?
items.e: The stop codon codes for no amino acid: 80.

items.q: A mRNA has a reading frame of 280 codons, the last being a stop codon. How many amino acids are in the polypeptide?
items.e: The stop codon codes for no amino acid: 279.

items.q: A gene is 1 500 bases long, of which 600 bases are in introns. How many amino acids does it code for? (Ignore start and stop codons.)
items.e: Only exons are translated: 900 bases ÷ 3 = 300.

items.q: A mRNA has a reading frame of 282 codons, the last being a stop codon. How many amino acids are in the polypeptide?
items.e: The stop codon codes for no amino acid: 281.

items.q: mRNA: AAAACUGUU. Codons: AAA = Lys, ACU = Thr, GUU = Val, AGC = Ser, CUU = Leu. What is the amino acid sequence?
items.e: Read the mRNA in triplets from the start: AAA ACU GUU.

items.q: What happens during translation?
c: ribosomes read mRNA codons and tRNA brings the matching amino acids
items.e: Peptide bonds join the amino acids.

items.q: What is the role of tRNA?
c: it carries the genetic code out of the nucleus
it carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon that pairs with the mRNA codon
items.e: The anticodon is complementary to the codon.

items.q: A DNA template strand has the sequence GACTCAGGCTCC. What is the sequence of the mRNA made from it?
items.e: mRNA is complementary to the template, with U instead of T.

items.q: A mRNA has a reading frame of 120 codons, the last being a stop codon. How many amino acids are in the polypeptide?
items.e: The stop codon codes for no amino acid: 119.

items.q: What happens during transcription?
c: DNA is copied before cell division
amino acids are joined at the ribosome
a mRNA copy of a gene is made from the DNA template strand in the nucleus
items.e: RNA polymerase does this.

items.q: A gene is 1 800 bases long, of which 150 bases are in introns. How many amino acids does it code for? (Ignore start and stop codons.)
items.e: Only exons are translated: 1 650 bases ÷ 3 = 550.

items.q: What is a promoter?
c: a DNA sequence near the start of a gene where RNA polymerase binds
items.e: Transcription factors help RNA polymerase bind.

items.q: What are introns?
c: the coding sections that stay in mRNA
non-coding sections of a gene that are removed from pre-mRNA
items.e: The exons are joined in splicing.

items.q: Which tRNA anticodon pairs with the mRNA codon AUU?
items.e: The anticodon is complementary to the codon: A–U and G–C.

items.q: A DNA template strand has the sequence CTGAAACAACTG. What is the sequence of the mRNA made from it?
items.e: mRNA is complementary to the template, with U instead of T.

items.q: Which tRNA anticodon pairs with the mRNA codon AAU?
items.e: The anticodon is complementary to the codon: A–U and G–C.

items.q: A DNA template strand has the sequence GCCGCAGCC. What is the sequence of the mRNA made from it?
items.e: mRNA is complementary to the template, with U instead of T.

items.q: mRNA: CAUAUUGCU. Codons: AUU = Ile, CAU = His, GCU = Ala, AGC = Ser, GUU = Val. What is the amino acid sequence?
items.e: Read the mRNA in triplets from the start: CAU AUU GCU.

items.q: mRNA: AUGAGCUGU. Codons: AGC = Ser, AUG = Met, UGU = Cys, UAU = Tyr. What is the amino acid sequence?
items.e: Read the mRNA in triplets from the start: AUG AGC UGU.

items.q: Which mutation is most likely to change many amino acids?
items.e: Every codon after it is changed.

items.q: A DNA template strand has the sequence TCGCGGTATACT. What is the sequence of the mRNA made from it?
items.e: mRNA is complementary to the template, with U instead of T.

items.q: mRNA: AGCGGCAUU. Codons: AGC = Ser, AUU = Ile, GGC = Gly, GGU = Gly. What is the amino acid sequence?
items.e: Read the mRNA in triplets from the start: AGC GGC AUU.

items.q: What is a homologous pair of chromosomes?
c: two chromosomes with the same genes at the same loci
a pair of sex chromosomes only
items.e: One comes from each parent.

items.q: What does RNA polymerase do?
c: joins RNA nucleotides complementary to the template strand
items.e: It moves along the gene.

items.q: A DNA template strand has the sequence TACGAGCGCGCT. What is the sequence of the mRNA made from it?
items.e: mRNA is complementary to the template, with U instead of T.

items.q: A DNA template strand has the sequence TCTAGGATGCTG. What is the sequence of the mRNA made from it?
items.e: mRNA is complementary to the template, with U instead of T.

items.q: A DNA template strand has the sequence TCTCATATT. What is the sequence of the mRNA made from it?
items.e: mRNA is complementary to the template, with U instead of T.

items.q: mRNA: AUUCAUAAA. Codons: AAA = Lys, AUU = Ile, CAU = His, GCA = Ala, CCU = Pro. What is the amino acid sequence?
items.e: Read the mRNA in triplets from the start: AUU CAU AAA.

items.q: mRNA: CAUCCUCCU. Codons: CAU = His, CCU = Pro, GGC = Gly, AUU = Ile. What is the amino acid sequence?
items.e: Read the mRNA in triplets from the start: CAU CCU CCU.

items.q: mRNA: GAUUUCGGC. Codons: GAU = Asp, GGC = Gly, UUC = Phe, GGU = Gly, GCA = Ala. What is the amino acid sequence?
items.e: Read the mRNA in triplets from the start: GAU UUC GGC.

items.q: mRNA: UUUCGUGGC. Codons: CGU = Arg, GGC = Gly, UUU = Phe, UAU = Tyr, AUU = Ile. What is the amino acid sequence?
items.e: Read the mRNA in triplets from the start: UUU CGU GGC.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 1 500 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 550, 900. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 1 500): 600, 550, 350. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: How is DNA profiling used in forensic science?
c: comparing the lengths of short tandem repeats from crime-scene DNA and suspects
reading a person's whole genome every time
items.e: STR patterns are almost unique to each person.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 4 000 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 2 100. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 4 000): 2 100, 1 900. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: What are the three temperature steps in each PCR cycle?
items.e: A heat-stable polymerase (Taq) is used.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 1 200 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 550, 650, 850. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 1 200): 550, 350, 200, 100. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 2 400 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 800. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 2 400): 1 600, 800. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 2 400 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 200, 2 150. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 2 400): 1 950, 250, 200. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 4 000 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 2 100, 3 750. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 4 000): 2 100, 1 650, 250. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 2 000 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 1 800. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 2 000): 1 800, 200. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 1 500 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 850. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 1 500): 850, 650. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 1 200 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 800. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 1 200): 800, 400. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 2 400 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 1 100. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 2 400): 1 300, 1 100. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: What do restriction endonucleases do?
c: cut DNA at specific recognition sequences
items.e: Many leave sticky ends.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 3 000 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 2 200, 2 500, 2 850. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 3 000): 2 200, 350, 300, 150. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 1 500 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 100, 1 100, 1 250. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 1 500): 1 000, 250, 150, 100. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: What is personalised medicine?
c: treatment chosen to suit a person's genome
items.e: Genome sequencing makes it possible.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 3 000 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 1 100. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 3 000): 1 900, 1 100. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 2 400 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 600. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 2 400): 1 800, 600. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 2 000 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 850, 1 200. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 2 000): 850, 800, 350. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: Why is a promoter added with a gene in genetic engineering?
c: so RNA polymerase can bind and the gene is transcribed
items.e: A terminator is added to stop it.
